prompt: How many write units does a `put-item` of a 3,500-byte item cost?
hint: 1 KB per unit, rounded up.

prompt: How many read units does a strongly consistent `get-item` of a 9,025-byte item cost?
hint: 4 KB per unit, rounded up.

prompt: The same 9,025-byte item is written inside a transaction. How many write units?
hint: Round first, then apply the multiplier.

choices.text: 18, twice the 9 units of a plain write
choices.why: Right: 9,025 bytes is 9 units, doubled.

choices.text: 9, as for any write of it
choices.why: That is a plain put. A transaction doubles it.

choices.text: 4.5, since a transaction is eventually consistent
choices.why: Consistency halves reads, never writes, and transactions are the expensive kind.

choices.text: 6, the transactional read price
choices.why: Six is what reading it in a transaction costs: 3 units, doubled.

prompt: moto reported 1.0 capacity unit for the put of the 9,025-byte item. What does that number tell you about AWS?
hint: What did moto answer for every other write?

choices.text: That AWS would charge one unit too
choices.why: AWS would charge 9. moto's number is the same for every write.

choices.text: That the item was compressed to under 1 KB
choices.why: DynamoDB charges on the item's size as written; nothing compresses it for billing.

choices.text: Nothing: it is a constant
choices.why: Right: moto gives every write that number. Units are counted by hand or by a program, never read off moto.

prompt: On demand in sa-east-1, how many dollars do 10 million writes of items up to 1 KB cost?
hint: The price sheet gives the price per million write request units.

prompt: A new table goes live next week and nobody knows its load. Which mode, and why?
hint: What does each mode do when the guess is wrong?

choices.text: Provisioned at a generous number, because provisioned units are cheaper
choices.why: Cheaper only when busy; a generous guess is idle capacity billed every hour.

choices.text: Provisioned at 1 unit, raised when the first throttle appears
choices.why: The first throttle is a customer's failed request.

choices.text: On demand: it cannot be under-provisioned and costs nothing while idle
choices.why: Right. Move to provisioned once a load has been measured.

prompt: moto switched the products table between provisioned and on demand three times in a minute. What does that show about AWS?
hint: Which limits did the section say moto does not have?

choices.text: That AWS allows it too, since the API is the same
choices.why: The same API with different limits behind it; this is exactly where moto stops imitating.

choices.text: Nothing: AWS limits it, and moto does not
choices.why: Right. AWS allows a limited number of switches to on demand in 24 hours; a success from moto says only that the request was well formed.

choices.text: That the limits apply only to tables with indexes
choices.why: The products table has no index, and the limits are per table regardless.

choices.text: That a switch takes effect only after the table is idle
choices.why: A switch takes effect at once; how often is the limit.

prompt: At what utilisation, in percent to one decimal place, do provisioned and on-demand writes cost the same in sa-east-1?
hint: A WCU-hour against the on-demand price of the 3,600 writes it can carry.

prompt: Why is provisioned 41% of the on-demand price for the steady load of 200 writes a second?
hint: Compare its utilisation with the break-even.

choices.text: Because provisioned capacity has a discount above 200 units
choices.why: There is no volume discount in the sheet; the first 25 units are free and the rest cost the same.

choices.text: Because on demand charges twice for writes at night
choices.why: On-demand prices do not change with the hour.

choices.text: Because autoscaling lowered it at night
choices.why: A steady load has nothing to follow; following it gave the same 200.77.

choices.text: Its units are 70% busy, well above 28.9%
choices.why: Right: 28.9% is where the two cost the same, and busy capacity is where provisioned wins.

prompt: For the spiky load, perfect autoscaling would cost 61.31 dollars and on demand 147.83. Why does the section still lean towards on demand?
hint: When does autoscaling act?

choices.text: Because autoscaling reacts minutes after load arrives, so a sudden spike is throttled first
choices.why: Right. A spike at a known time can be met with scheduled scaling; an unexpected one is what on demand is for.

choices.text: Because 61.31 is below the free tier
choices.why: The free allowance is 25 units, which this load passes in every hour.

choices.text: Because provisioned tables cannot exceed 1,000 units
choices.why: The 1,000 is per partition, not per table.

prompt: Provisioned at 1,429 units all month, the spiky load costs 1,003.16 dollars. Where does most of that money go?
hint: What do the units do at 20 writes a second?

choices.text: Into units that sit idle for 23 hours a day
choices.why: Right: at 20 writes a second they are 1.4% used.

choices.text: Into the writes of the evening promotion
choices.why: One hour of 24; the other 23 are paid for too.

choices.text: Into storage, which provisioned tables pay for by the unit
choices.why: Storage is billed per GB in both modes, and the program counts none.

choices.text: Into the retries of throttled writes
choices.why: With capacity for the peak all day, nothing is throttled.

prompt: What does DynamoDB autoscaling change?
hint: It drives an `update-table` on your behalf.

choices.text: The number of partitions
choices.why: Partitions are DynamoDB's business and are never set by anybody.

choices.text: The billing mode, switching to on demand at peaks
choices.why: It never changes the mode, and the mode has its own limits.

choices.text: An on-demand table's price per million requests
choices.why: On demand has nothing to scale; autoscaling applies to provisioned tables only.

choices.text: Capacity units, within set bounds
choices.why: Right: a provisioned table's, within its scalable target, here between 5 and 500 write units.

prompt: Which of these are true of the four alarms moto created for the write policy? Choose every one.
hint: Compare their metric names and thresholds with the table.

choices.text: They name read metrics for a policy on write units
choices.why: Yes, `ConsumedReadCapacityUnits` on every one.

choices.text: The high alarm needs 2 one-minute periods, the low one 15
choices.why: Yes, which is the shape AWS uses: out quickly, in slowly.

choices.text: Their thresholds were computed from the table's 5 write units
choices.why: 42 and 30 are 70% and 50% of 60 seconds of one unit.

choices.text: One of them will fire during `flood.py`
choices.why: moto publishes no metrics, so no alarm ever fires.

prompt: A policy that keeps consumed units near 70% of the provisioned ones is a target ___ policy.
hint: It follows a target.

prompt: A provisioned table has 10,000 write units, and every write uses the partition key `2026-10-16`. Roughly how many writes a second can it take?
hint: Where does one partition key live?

choices.text: About 1,000, one partition's limit
choices.why: Right, whatever the table has. That is a hot partition.

choices.text: 10,000, the table's capacity
choices.why: The table's capacity is spread over partitions, and one key uses one.

choices.text: 20,000, with adaptive capacity doubling it
choices.why: Adaptive capacity lends unused capacity to a busy partition but does not lift the ceiling on one key.

choices.text: 3,000, the partition's read limit
choices.why: Writes have their own limit, a third of that.

prompt: The index `by-day` is sharded into `2026-10-16#0` to `#9`. What does the back office's "every order of a day" become?
hint: Who pays for spreading the writes?

choices.text: One query on `2026-10-16`, which still finds all ten keys
choices.why: A query takes one exact partition key; `2026-10-16` alone is now none of them.

choices.text: A scan of the index filtered on the day
choices.why: That would read every day in the index to find one.

choices.text: Ten queries, one per suffix, whose answers the reader merges into one list
choices.why: Right. The writes are spread and the read pays for it.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since DynamoDB strips the suffix
choices.why: DynamoDB knows nothing of the convention; the suffix is part of the key.

prompt: `flood.py` wrote 5,000 items to a table of 5 write units with 0 retries. What can be concluded about the design?
hint: What did moto do with the capacity?

choices.text: That 5 units are enough for 5,000 writes in a few seconds
choices.why: They would carry about 5 a second, plus burst; moto ignored the capacity.

choices.text: That burst capacity covered the whole run
choices.why: Burst is at most five minutes of unused capacity, 1,500 writes here, and moto has none.

choices.text: Nothing about DynamoDB: moto never throttles, so the run measured the program and the laptop
choices.why: Right. Capacity is checked with the arithmetic, and on a real account.

prompt: Match each operation on a 6 KB item with its units on AWS.
hint: 6 KB is 6 write blocks and 2 read blocks.

prompt: On AWS, put the events of a sudden surge on an autoscaled table in order.
hint: The alarm needs two minutes of data.
items: Writes jump to three times the provisioned capacity
Burst capacity absorbs the first of them
Requests are throttled and the SDK retries them
The high alarm fires after two minutes above the target
Application Auto Scaling raises the table's capacity

prompt: Quitanda's stock table takes 300 writes a second from the warehouse scanners, 7 to 19 every day, and almost nothing at night. Which is the cheapest sound choice?
hint: Work out the utilisation of each option against 28.9%.

choices.text: Provisioned for 300 a second around the clock
choices.why: Busy 12 hours of 24 at most, 70% of that: 35% averaged, barely above break-even, and the nights are waste.

choices.text: On demand, because any load with a quiet night is spiky
choices.why: The load is predictable to the hour; that is the case scheduled capacity is for.

choices.text: Provisioned, scheduled up before 7 and down after 19
choices.why: Right, with autoscaling in between. A known pattern lets provisioned capacity be busy while it is paid for.

choices.text: Provisioned at 1 unit, letting burst capacity carry the day
choices.why: Burst is five minutes of unused capacity, not a day of it.
